name: Lima
tagline: A Pacific capital crowned by the world's finest kitchens.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Oct, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: December to April is bright, warm and beach-ready; May to November brings the grey garua fog, though October's processions and the food calendar reward a visit.

ourTake.lede: Lima is a food city first, most people rush it on the way to Cusco and miss the point entirely. Give it two full days, base in Barranco or Miraflores on the cliff, and build the trip around lunch tables rather than sights. The Historic Centre is worth one focused morning; the rest of your time belongs to the coast and the kitchens.
ourTake.comeIf: You came to Peru for the food and want a few nights in the world's finest kitchens before Machu Picchu.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a beach or a self-contained resort week; Lima is a working coastal capital, not a place to unwind for seven days.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Belmond Miraflores Park
items.description: An all-suite tower set in a green garden atop the Miraflores cliff, its rooftop pool floating over the Pacific, the city's most complete grand-hotel address.

items.name: Country Club Lima Hotel
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A 1927 hacienda-style landmark, declared a national monument, colonial arches, a serious Peruvian art collection and steps from the Lima Golf Club.

items.name: Hotel B
items.description: A restored 1914 Belle Époque mansion in bohemian Barranco, hung with contemporary Peruvian art, the city's most characterful small luxury house.

items.name: JW Marriott Hotel Lima
items.description: A glass tower on the Miraflores clifftop, every room facing the Pacific, polished, reliable, big-hotel service above the Costa Verde.

items.name: Hilton Lima Miraflores
items.description: A sleek modern tower in the heart of Miraflores with a rooftop pool and hot tubs, well-run, contemporary comfort near the boardwalk.

items.name: Villa Barranco by Ananay Hotels
items.description: A restored 1920s republican townhouse of just nine rooms, near the ocean in Barranco's arts district, boho-chic character behind heritage walls.

items.name: The Westin Lima Hotel & Convention Center
items.description: Peru's tallest building, a glass tower in the financial district with a heated indoor pool, spa and sweeping city views.

items.name: AC Hotel Lima Miraflores
items.description: Marriott's design-forward European brand in central Miraflores, clean, contemporary rooms and a rooftop bar over the district.

items.name: Plaza Mayor (Plaza de Armas)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Lima
items.description: The founding square of Lima, laid out by Pizarro in 1535 and framed by the Cathedral, the ochre Government Palace and the balconied Municipal Palace. A private guide turns one walkable block into two centuries of viceregal drama; the changing of the guard at the palace at noon is the set-piece.

items.name: Lima Cathedral
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Lima
items.description: The city's mother church, begun in 1535 and rebuilt after earthquakes, its carved-wood choir stalls and the tomb of Pizarro himself set behind glass in a side chapel. A quiet, air-conditioned half hour on the Plaza Mayor that even restless grandchildren settle into.

items.name: Government Palace & Changing of the Guard
items.description: The Casa de Pizarro, official residence of Peru's president, whose ceremonial changing of the guard each day at noon draws a scarlet-and-brass parade in the forecourt. A guided visit inside, arranged ahead, reveals the gilded state rooms behind the facade.

items.name: Monastery of San Francisco & the Catacombs
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Lima
items.description: A butter-yellow baroque church whose underground bone-lined catacombs held tens of thousands of colonial burials, the skulls and femurs still arranged in geometric wells. Upstairs, a monumental 25,000-volume antique library rewards the reader in the family; the descent is not for the very young or claustrophobic.

items.name: Basilica & Convent of Santo Domingo
items.description: The 16th-century Dominican complex that cradled the Americas' oldest university (San Marcos) and holds the relics of Peru's two great saints, Rose of Lima and Martín de Porres. Tiled cloisters and a climbable bell tower make it the calmer, less-touristed twin to San Francisco.

items.name: Casa de Aliaga
items.description: A colonial mansion continuously inhabited by the same family since 1535, one of the oldest lived-in houses in the Americas, its baroque Golden Room and painted ceilings shown by private appointment. A rare, discreet look behind Lima's viceregal facades, best arranged through your advisor.

items.name: Torre Tagle Palace
items.description: The finest surviving 18th-century mansion in the city, its Andalusian-baroque doorway crowned by two intricately carved cedar-and-mahogany Moorish balconies. Now Peru's foreign ministry, so admired chiefly from the street, a two-minute stop that photographers linger over.

items.name: Casa Museo de Barranco murals & street art walk
items.description: Lima's bohemian quarter is an open-air gallery of murals splashed across republican mansions and cobbled alleys, best read with a local guide who knows the artists. An unhurried, camera-friendly hour that suits teenagers and design-minded travellers alike.

items.name: Puente de los Suspiros (Bridge of Sighs)
items.description: A little wooden footbridge over a leafy ravine, wrapped in a wish-making legend, cross without breathing and your wish comes true, with the Pacific glinting at the end of the lane. The romantic heart of Barranco, loveliest at golden hour before dinner.

items.name: MATE, Museo Mario Testino
items.description: The Peruvian fashion photographer's museum in a restored 19th-century townhouse, pairing his Kate Moss and Diana portraits with a room of traditional Andean dress. A tight, stylish hour that lands especially well with fashion-literate families.

items.name: Museo Pedro de Osma
items.description: A jewel-box collection of viceregal painting, silver and Cusco-school art in an Art Nouveau seaside villa with formal gardens. Small, serene and beautifully hung, the connoisseur's museum, and a cool refuge on a bright Barranco afternoon.

items.name: Barranco bars & pisco cocktails
items.description: After dark the quarter's republican mansions turn into design bars, Ayahuasca's Andean-glam rooms among them, pouring pisco cocktails and live jazz. A grown-up evening with a driver on call, a short hop from the coastal restaurants.

items.name: El Malecón cliff-top parks
items.description: A ribbon of manicured gardens running along the Miraflores clifftops high above the Pacific, threaded with sculpture, joggers and paragliders overhead. The city's favourite sunset stroll, buggy- and grandparent-friendly, with the ocean always in view.

items.name: Parque del Amor
items.description: A clifftop garden built around Víctor Delfín's giant mosaic sculpture of embracing lovers, its curving Gaudí-style benches inlaid with lines of Peruvian love poetry. One of Lima's best-placed sunset perches, and a favourite family photo stop.

items.name: Larcomar
items.description: An open-air mall carved into the cliff face below the Malecón, its terraces of restaurants, cinemas and shops hanging over the surf. Handy for a late lunch or a gift for the family with the Pacific as backdrop; less a sight than a comfortable pause.

items.name: Huaca Pucllana
items.description: A great adobe pyramid of the pre-Inca Lima culture, built of millions of hand-shaped bricks and rising unexpectedly amid the smart residential streets. The floodlit evening tour, followed by dinner at the on-site restaurant beside the ruin, is pure Lima theatre.

items.name: Paragliding over the Miraflores cliffs
items.description: Tandem flights launch off the Malecón and soar along the coast on the sea breeze, the whole city and the Pacific unrolling beneath you. A ten-minute thrill for the bolder travellers, easily watched from the parks by those who would rather keep their feet down.

items.name: Parque Kennedy & the cats
items.description: The buzzing central square of Miraflores, ringed by cafés and famous for the dozens of well-fed stray cats who lounge on its lawns. A gentle, easy stop for children and an antidote to museum fatigue, with churro carts nearby.

items.name: Amano Textile Museum
items.description: A private, appointment-based collection of pre-Columbian textiles, Paracas embroideries and Chancay lace among them, displayed with near-museum quiet in a Miraflores house. Intimate and expert, the thread-lover's Lima; guided so the delicacy of the weaving lands.

items.name: Lugar de la Memoria (LUM)
items.description: A striking clifftop museum dedicated to the victims of Peru's 1980s–90s internal conflict, its multimedia galleries sober and beautifully sited above the sea. A serious, moving hour for adults and older teens; free to enter, never crowded.

items.name: Larco Museum
items.description: A pre-Columbian treasure house in an 18th-century mansion wrapped in bougainvillea gardens, gold and silver of the Moche kings, a walk-through storage vault, and the famously frank erotic ceramics gallery (skippable with young children). The café on the terrace makes it an easy half-day for all ages.

items.name: Museo de Arte de Lima (MALI)
items.description: Peru's leading art museum in a grand 1870s exhibition palace, tracing 3,000 years from Paracas textiles to modern Peruvian masters across 18,000 works. A civilised, well-curated hour a short drive from the Plaza Mayor, easily paced for grandparents.

items.name: Museo Nacional de Arqueología, Antropología e Historia
items.description: Peru's oldest and largest museum, in a colonial mansion once home to the liberators San Martín and Bolívar, holding the carved Raimondi Stele and a fine scale model of Machu Picchu. The best primer before the Sacred Valley, and a five-minute walk from the Larco.

items.name: MUNA, Museo Nacional del Perú
items.description: Peru's vast new national museum, a sweeping concrete landmark beside the Pachacamac ruins south of the city, guardian of half a million artefacts from 5,000 years of pre-Columbian civilisation. Pair it with the ruins for a full, uncrowded archaeology day with a private driver.

items.name: Gold Museum of Peru (Museo Oro del Perú)
items.description: A private collection glittering with Moche, Chimú and Lambayeque goldwork, funerary masks and ceremonial knives, alongside a large historic-arms gallery upstairs. A dazzling, slightly old-world hour in a quiet residential district, treasure that impresses every generation.

items.name: Circuito Mágico del Agua (Magic Water Circuit)
credentials: Guinness World Record, largest fountain complex in a public park
items.description: Thirteen illuminated fountains, some to run through, one a 120-metre tunnel of water, culminating in a nightly laser-and-music show across a colossal jet. Guinness-recognised as the world's largest fountain complex in a park, and a guaranteed hit with children after dark.

items.name: Barrio Chino (Chinatown) & the chifas
items.description: The oldest Chinatown in Latin America, entered under a red paifang gate on Calle Capón, where century-old chifas serve the Chinese-Peruvian fusion, lomo saltado, arroz chaufa, woven into the national kitchen. A lively, flavour-led walk best done with a food guide who knows the good doors.

items.name: Central
items.description: Virgilio Martínez's altitude-themed tasting journey up the ecosystems of Peru, from ocean floor to high Andes, backed by the Mater research kitchen, crowned the World's Best Restaurant in 2023. Book months ahead; a plant-forward menu can be arranged for vegetarian guests.

items.name: Maido
items.description: Mitsuharu Tsumura's Nikkei masterwork, Japanese precision married to Amazonian and Pacific ingredients across a long tasting menu, named the World's Best Restaurant in 2025. The city's hardest table; a warm 'Maido!' greets you at the door, and dietary needs are handled with grace.

items.name: Kjolle
credentials: World's 50 Best Restaurants, Pía León named World's Best Female Chef
items.description: Pía León's own restaurant beside Central in the Casa Tupac compound, a colour-drenched celebration of native Peruvian ingredients from the woman named the World's Best Female Chef. A more relaxed but no less brilliant table for the design-and-food set.

items.name: Mérito
items.description: A small, buzzy Barranco kitchen of Venezuelan-Peruvian cooking that has climbed the world lists on the strength of pure flavour rather than spectacle. The insider's dinner, intimate, unfussy and easier to book than the giants.

items.name: Mayta
items.description: Jaime Pesaque's refined take on modern Peruvian, drawing on ingredients from coast, Andes and Amazon in a sleek Miraflores room. A polished, reliable fine-dining choice when the top two tables are full.

items.name: Ceviche at a cevichería
items.description: Lima's defining dish, raw fish 'cooked' in lime with chilli and red onion, chased with a shot of the leche de tigre marinade, eaten at a bustling lunchtime cevichería. The essential first meal in the city; ask your guide for the vegetarian causa and criollo sides alongside.

items.name: Pisco sour tasting or masterclass
items.description: The national cocktail, pisco, lime, sugar, egg white and bitters, shaken to a foamy crown, learned hands-on in a beachfront class or savoured at a great bar. A convivial, all-ages activity (mocktail versions for younger travellers) and a fine primer on Peru's grape spirit.

items.name: Mercado de Surquillo food tour
items.description: A real neighbourhood market piled with Amazonian fruits, sea bass, aji chillies and unfamiliar tubers, best explored with a chef or guide who lets you taste as you go. A vivid, grounding morning, and where many of the great restaurants shop.

items.name: Costa Verde beaches & the surf
items.description: The pebbly beaches at the foot of Lima's cliffs, where surfers ride the swell year-round below Miraflores and Barranco. More for the seaside drive, a beachfront lunch and watching the waves than for swimming, an easy, low-key coastal hour.

items.name: Pachacamac archaeological site
items.description: A sprawling pre-Inca and Inca pilgrimage city of pyramids and temples on a bluff above the Pacific, an easy half-day south of the centre with its own excellent site museum. The most rewarding ruins near Lima; a private guide and driver make light work of the distances.

items.name: Islas Palomino sea-lion swim
items.description: A boat from the old port of Callao out to rocky islets where a colony of thousands of sea lions lives, with a wetsuit-clad swim among the curious pups the highlight. A salt-and-adrenaline half-day for confident swimmers, a nearer stand-in for the Ballestas.

items.name: Callao Monumental & La Punta
items.description: The once-rough port district's historic core, reborn as a street-art and gallery quarter, with the genteel sea-facing promenade of La Punta nearby and the star-shaped Real Felipe fortress guarding the bay. An offbeat, guided afternoon for travellers who have already ticked the classics.

items.name: Ballestas Islands & Paracas Reserve (day trip)
items.description: The 'poor man's Galápagos', a boat among islands teeming with sea lions, Humboldt penguins and vast seabird colonies, past the giant Candelabra geoglyph, then the red-sand cliffs of the Paracas desert reserve. A long but spectacular day around three hours south; best as a private car-and-boat charter.

items.name: Sacred City of Caral (day trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Sacred City of Caral-Supe
items.description: The oldest city in the Americas, 5,000-year-old sunken plazas and earthen pyramids that rose contemporary with Egypt's, set in a green valley north of Lima. A profound, uncrowded full day for the history-minded; roughly three hours each way, so a private driver is essential.

items.name: Barranco to Chorrillos coastal walk & the fisherman's pier
items.description: South of Barranco the clifftop path drops to Chorrillos, where a small working fishing harbour, the Regatas beach club and fresh-off-the-boat ceviche shacks give a more local seaside afternoon. A relaxed, guided coastal ramble away from the tourist core.

items.name: Maido
credentials: The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025, No.1 (The World's Best Restaurant)
Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024, No.2 (Best Restaurant in Peru)
items.description: Mitsuharu 'Micha' Tsumura's Nikkei masterwork, Japanese precision married to Peru's Amazon and Pacific, and, as of 2025, the best restaurant on earth.

items.name: Central
credentials: The World's 50 Best Restaurants, No.1 in 2023, now in the Best of the Best hall of fame
Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants, inducted to Best of the Best hall of fame
items.description: Virgilio Martínez and Pía León's journey through Peru by altitude, ingredients from the ocean floor to the high Andes, plated as a map of a country.

items.name: Kjolle
items.description: Pía León's own restaurant beside Central, bright, colourful, ingredient-led cooking that made her one of the most celebrated chefs in Latin America.

items.name: Mérito
items.description: A small Barranco room where Venezuelan and Peruvian roots meet, Juan Luis Martínez's inventive, personal cooking on an intimate scale.

items.name: Mayta
items.description: Jaime Pesaque's polished flagship, Peruvian ingredients from coast, sierra and jungle through a refined, technical lens.

items.name: Rafael
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024, No.19 (Highest Climber)
items.description: Rafael Osterling's long-loved room, a diverse menu drawing on Peruvian heritage and Nikkei, and the Highest Climber of 2024.

items.name: Cosme
items.description: James Berckemeyer's bright, sustainability-minded kitchen, Peruvian comfort cooking, elevated and served with ease.

items.name: La Mar Cebichería
items.description: Gastón Acurio's landmark cevichería, the benchmark for Lima ceviche, made to fine-dining standard in a buzzing daytime room.

items.name: Astrid y Gastón
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants, inaugural No.1 (2013); long-standing list mainstay
items.description: The restaurant that started it all, Gastón Acurio and Astrid Gutsche's flagship in a grand San Isidro hacienda, the cradle of modern Peruvian dining.

items.name: Osso
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024, No.17 (extended top 100)
items.description: Renzo Garibaldi's butcher-restaurant, dry-aged meats and charcuterie at a level that draws serious carnivores across the city.

items.name: Fiesta
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024, No.39 (extended top 100)
items.description: Chef Héctor Solís's ode to the northern cuisine of Chiclayo, bold, regional Peruvian cooking rarely found at this level in the capital.

items.name: Maras, The Westin Lima
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide (within The Westin Lima)
items.description: Rafael Piqueras's refined hotel dining room, modern Peruvian cooking with strong technique in a polished setting.

items.name: Isolina
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024, No.24 (extended top 100)
items.description: Generous, old-school Lima taberna cooking, hearty portions of the city's home dishes in a warm, bustling Barranco room.

items.name: El Bodegón
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants, 50 Best Discovery (Acurio group)
items.description: Gastón Acurio's warm bodega, classic criollo home cooking and grilled dishes in an easy, tavern-like setting.

items.name: Panchita
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants, 50 Best Discovery (Acurio group)
items.description: Gastón Acurio's anticucho and grill house, Peruvian street-food classics, especially the skewers, done with real polish.

items.name: Ayahuasca
credentials: A restored Barranco mansion, the city's most atmospheric bar setting
items.description: A rambling, beautifully restored 19th-century mansion in Barranco, countless rooms of period detail, pisco cocktails and a genuine sense of place.

items.name: Museo del Pisco
credentials: The city's reference bar for pisco, Peru's national spirit
items.description: A living museum to Peru's national spirit, dozens of piscos and every variation on the pisco sour, in a lively Barranco room.

items.name: Bar Inglés, Country Club Lima Hotel
credentials: Within The Leading Hotels of the World, a heritage hotel bar
items.description: The clubby, wood-panelled English bar of the 1927 Country Club hotel, polished pisco sours under a serious Peruvian art collection.

items.name: Lady Bee
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars 2025, No.13 (and Michter's Art of Hospitality Award 2025)
items.description: Alonso Palomino and Gabriela León's product-driven bar, Amazonian fruits, Andean potatoes and pisco turned into some of the world's finest drinks.

items.name: Carnaval
items.description: Aaron Díaz's meticulously built temple to the cocktail in upscale San Isidro, a seven-drink 'Gran Carnaval' tasting of house specialities.

items.name: Insumo
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery (Lima)
items.description: An ingredient-obsessed cocktail bar from an alumnus of the city's best kitchens, precise, produce-led drinks in an intimate Barranco room.

items.name: Cala
credentials: Beachfront setting on the Costa Verde, the city's premier sunset drink
items.description: A glass pavilion right on the Barranco beachfront, cocktails and Pacific sunsets at the water's edge below the cliffs.

plan.heading: 3 days in Lima, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into Hotel B, the belle-époque mansion in Barranco, and walk the Bridge of Sighs to the cliffs.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: See the MATE and MAC galleries, then the Pacific light along the Malecón.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Central, Virgilio Martínez's ecosystem-by-altitude menu, ranked among the world's very best.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Walk the Miraflores clifftops and the Huaca Pucllana adobe pyramid rising among the streets.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private ceviche and pisco session, then the coastal parks at Larcomar.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Maido, Mitsuharu Tsumura's Nikkei tasting menu, a 50 Best fixture.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Larco Museum's pre-Columbian gold and ceramics, set in a colonial villa.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The colonial centre, Plaza Mayor, San Francisco's catacombs and cloisters.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A relaxed final dinner at Kjolle, Pía León's own kitchen next to Central.

neighbourhoods.heading: Where to base yourself
neighbourhoods.pairWith: Cusco, Buenos Aires, Rio de Janeiro

items.name: Barranco
items.description: Bohemian, walkable and full of galleries and bars; best for atmosphere and the best restaurants.

items.name: Miraflores
items.description: Polished cliff-top district with parks and hotels; the safe, convenient default.

items.name: San Isidro
items.description: Leafy, quiet and residential; suits travellers who want calm over nightlife.

events.name: Mistura Food Festival
events.note: Latin America's largest gastronomy fair, gathering the country's cooks and produce on the coast.

events.name: Señor de los Milagros (Lord of Miracles)
events.note: Purple-robed processions through the centre all month, the largest on 18 October.

events.name: Fiestas Patrias (Independence)
events.note: Two national holidays of parades and celebration across the capital.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in Miraflores or bohemian Barranco for the ocean air and the best tables; Lima's world-ranked restaurants (Central, Maido) book weeks ahead, so have them secured before you fly, and note the coast is often grey and cool from June to October.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Jorge Chávez International (LIM), now in its new terminal, with a private car meeting you for the 40 to 60-minute transfer to the coastal districts.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Traffic is heavy, so a private driver is the only civilised way across town; within Miraflores and Barranco you can walk the clifftops and streets.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM (Claro or Entel) gives solid 4G; wifi in the good hotels is dependable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the Peruvian sol; cards are widely accepted, keep some soles for smaller places, and tip around 10 percent.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Dec-Apr is warm and clear, the kind window; May-Oct sits under the coastal 'garua', a persistent grey sea-mist that greys out the city though it rarely rains.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; route via a European hub, KLM via Amsterdam or Air France via Paris to Lima, or Iberia/LATAM via Madrid, total around 24-26h. Fly the European carrier's business class on the long transatlantic leg; Amsterdam and Madrid both offer good connection times and lounges, so pick the itinerary with a 2-3h layover rather than the cheapest.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; Hepatitis A and typhoon cover advised, and yellow-fever only matters if combining with the Amazon. Lima sits at sea level, so no altitude concern (unlike Cusco). Drink bottled water. Miraflores, San Isidro and Barranco are safe; use vetted transport and avoid hailing street taxis.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Lima is a world food capital and increasingly veg-friendly; pure-veg is easy in Miraflores/Barranco, strict Jain needs advance notice. Good Indian options exist. Cebiche is fish-based, but strong vegetarian tasting menus are available at the top tables.
